contentBlocks.heading: Should Your IB PYP Tutor Provide Home Tutoring, or Meet Online?
contentBlocks.body:
Home tutoring is the right starting point for most families choosing an IB PYP tutor in Gurgaon: a young child settles faster in a familiar room with their own materials at hand, and a parent can observe quietly without disrupting the session. A tutor working at home also sees the actual reading books and unit-of-inquiry materials the child is using, which speeds up how closely sessions track the classroom.

Online lessons are a genuine alternative when travel is the obstacle, a family in Manesar on a weekday evening, a session that only fits a narrow window that week, or a family travelling outside Gurgaon briefly. A shared screen handles reading and simple maths comfortably, though a young child's focus fades faster online than in person, so sessions run shorter and the tutor has to work harder to keep things interactive minute to minute.

A hybrid pattern, home tutoring as the default with online filling gaps as needed, is what most families choosing a tutor through IB Gram settle into after the first month or so. It keeps materials and rapport consistent while giving a practical way out of a single clashing week without losing the session altogether, provided the default and the fallback are agreed once rather than argued over weekly.

What tends not to work for this age group is choosing a tutor who only offers online from day one. A young child who has never met the tutor in person often takes longer to warm to a screen-only relationship, so two or three home sessions first, before shifting balance if that suits the family, usually settles faster.

contentBlocks.heading: The Signs of a Genuine PYP Specialist
contentBlocks.body:
The most reliable sign is specificity. Ask a genuine PYP specialist what they would do in the first session with your child, and they name something concrete: reviewing the current unit's central idea, checking where the child's reading or number sense actually sits, planning one or two short activities around a real theme. A generalist tends to answer in generalities: "building confidence," "making it fun," "seeing what the child needs," phrases that sound reasonable but commit to nothing checkable.

A second sign is how a tutor talks about assessment. Because the PYP has no external examinations, a genuine specialist will not mention grades, marks or test scores when describing how they will track progress; they will talk instead about observable change, reading stamina, willingness to ask questions, confidence handling an open-ended problem. A tutor who keeps returning to test language for a PYP-age child either has not adjusted from a different curriculum or has not fully understood this one.

A third sign is comfort with the learner profile and transdisciplinary themes as working vocabulary rather than buzzwords memorised for an interview. Ask a tutor to name a recent unit they taught and describe, in a sentence, how it connected two different themes or attributes; a specialist answers naturally, while a tutor reciting the ten attributes from memory without connecting them to real teaching is performing rather than practising.

Red flags are just as informative as good signs. Be cautious of a tutor who promises a specific outcome for a five-year-old, who wants to start without asking about the current unit at all, or who cannot describe how a session with a distracted or upset child would actually go. None of these alone is disqualifying, but more than one together is a reason to see a different tutor before committing to a regular schedule.

contentBlocks.heading: Four Weeks In: Is the Tutor Actually Working Out?
contentBlocks.body:
By four weeks, a family should see specific, nameable change rather than a general sense that things are fine: more willingness to read aloud, steadier number work, a question about the current unit raised unprompted at home, or simply less resistance to starting the session. A tutor genuinely working out can point to two or three such moments when asked directly; one who cannot is worth questioning, whatever the general impression has been.

If nothing at all has shifted after a full month of consistent sessions, do not wait through a second month hoping it resolves itself. Sometimes a small adjustment, a different time of day, shorter activities, more connection to the current unit, fixes it; sometimes the honest conclusion is that this particular tutor is not the right specialist for this particular child, and IB Gram can offer an alternative.

Separate whether the child likes the tutor from whether the tutor is actually helping; the two often align but not always. A child who enjoys the sessions but shows no real change in reading or number confidence after a month is not necessarily making progress, and a child who complains mildly but is visibly more capable may be exactly where they should be. Ask about both directly rather than assuming enjoyment equals progress.

No tutor can guarantee a specific outcome, and one who does should be treated with more caution, not less. What a genuinely good match reliably offers is consistent, specific attention to a child's actual gaps, reviewed honestly every four to six weeks rather than left to run unexamined.

contentBlocks.heading: From First Query to Regular IB PYP Tuition in Gurgaon
contentBlocks.body:
Setting up IB PYP tuition in Gurgaon starts with a short intake, not a long form: which school, how old the child is, the current unit of inquiry if you know it, and whether you are picturing home tuition, online lessons or a mix of both. IB Gram uses that to shortlist a tutor who has actually worked inside the Primary Years Programme before, since a generalist primary tutor and a PYP specialist run very different sessions even when teaching the same reading or maths skill.

A free trial class comes next, at whichever mode you prefer, and it is worth treating as a proper look rather than a formality: watch how the tutor opens the session, how they respond when your child gets something wrong, and whether they can explain, in a sentence or two, how the lesson connects to the current transdisciplinary theme. If the trial goes well, sessions settle into a weekly rhythm, typically once or twice a week for a PYP-age child, adjusted after IB Gram checks in around the one-month mark.

Frequency is not fixed for the whole year. A child catching up on reading fluency midway through a unit might need two sessions a week for a few weeks, then step down to one once the gap has closed; a child broadly on track might use one session a week mainly to keep pace with each new unit of inquiry as it starts. A tutor who suggests the same frequency regardless of what the child actually needs is worth questioning.

Tuition through IB Gram is not billed or scheduled centrally session by session; the regular pattern is agreed between the family and tutor once the trial has confirmed fit, subject to tutor availability. IB Gram's part is the shortlisting, the verification behind it, and staying reachable if a family wants to review the tutor partway through.

contentBlocks.heading: The IB Primary Years Programme, in Plain Terms
contentBlocks.body:
The Primary Years Programme (PYP) covers ages 3 to 12 and is built around six transdisciplinary themes: Who we are; Where we are in place and time; How we express ourselves; How the world works; How we organize ourselves; and Sharing the planet. Each one runs as a unit of inquiry for several weeks, pulling subjects together rather than teaching them in separate periods, and every unit aims to build one or more of the ten attributes of the IB learner profile alongside the academic content.

There are no external examinations in the PYP, which is the single fact that should shape any tuition plan for this age group. Tuition here is not exam preparation; it is building the reading stamina, number sense and inquiry skills a unit assumes the child already has, and closing specific gaps before they compound into the next unit. A tutor who structures PYP tuition like exam coaching, with timed tests and mark schemes, is working against the programme rather than with it.

In the final year, students complete the PYP exhibition, a collaborative, student-led inquiry into a real issue that culminates in a presentation to the school community. Tuition in that year often shifts to support research skills, organisation and presentation practice around the exhibition, alongside whatever subject gaps remain, since the exhibition draws on everything the programme has built up over the preceding years.

Because assessment in the PYP is mostly teacher-observed rather than tested, a tuition plan cannot lean on past scores to show it is working. This is exactly why the trial lesson and the first month matter more here than they would for an older student with a term of test results to look back on: they are, in effect, the only real evidence a family has early on.

Three more: How the world works; How we organize ourselves; Sharing the planet.

contentBlocks.heading: What a PYP Specialist Actually Teaches Week to Week
contentBlocks.body:
A specialist PYP tutor's week looks different from a generalist's. Rather than a fixed English-then-Maths split, sessions often open with whatever the current unit of inquiry needs most that week: building vocabulary for a How the World Works unit on materials, say, or practising the kind of open-ended questioning the PYP expects a child to ask on their own. Literacy work stays tied to the child's actual phonics stage or reading level, and numeracy practice keeps the same open-ended, reasoning-first style the classroom uses rather than drilling isolated sums.

Session length and pacing matter more for this age than for an older student. A young child cannot hold focus for a long uninterrupted block, so a specialist tutor breaks a session into several shorter activities with a change of task or a short break between them, watching for the point where the child's attention genuinely drops rather than pushing through a fixed clock time regardless.

A generalist primary tutor, by contrast, often defaults to a textbook-led session with little reference to the unit of inquiry at all, which can still help with raw literacy or numeracy but leaves the child working in a different style from their classroom for an hour a week, week after week. Ask a prospective tutor directly how they would plan a session around a named unit; a vague answer is the clearest sign of a generalist rather than a specialist.

Exhibition-year tuition adds research and presentation skills to the weekly mix: helping the child narrow a broad question, find and organise information at an age-appropriate level, and rehearse explaining their thinking out loud, always stopping short of doing the research or the thinking for the child. This distinction between coaching the process and producing the content is worth raising directly with any tutor before the exhibition year begins.

contentBlocks.heading: How School Terms in Gurgaon Shape a Tuition Timetable
contentBlocks.body:
IB Gram is an independent platform and is not affiliated with any school named here, the International Baccalaureate, Cambridge International Education or Pearson Edexcel. Families whose children attend schools such as Pathways World School Aravali, Pathways School Gurgaon, Lancers International School, Scottish High International School, GD Goenka World School, Heritage Xperiential Learning School, The Shri Ram School Aravali or DPS International Edge are named here only for local context, not as a claim about any school's curriculum or programme.

A tuition timetable that ignores the school calendar quickly falls out of step. Units of inquiry typically run several weeks each, and a tuition plan should shift focus as each new unit opens rather than running the same content regardless of what the class is doing that fortnight. Term breaks, festival holidays and the run-up to the PYP exhibition in the final year all compress the weeks around them, and a fixed weekly slot that never flexes tends to clash with exactly these periods.

Parents are usually the quickest route for a tutor to learn a unit has changed, since tuition arranged through IB Gram has no direct channel into the school. A brief note after parent-teacher meetings, saying what the teacher flagged and what the next unit is, does more for a session's usefulness than almost anything else a family can do.

Building two or three review points into the year, roughly aligned with school reporting periods, keeps tuition responsive rather than running on autopilot for months at a stretch. A tutor and family who only ever talk about the schedule and never about what has actually changed at school tend to drift out of sync by the second term.

contentBlocks.heading: Home Tuition, Online or Hybrid: What Works for PYP Learners?
contentBlocks.body:
Home tuition is the strongest starting point for most PYP-age children, because a familiar room with their own books and materials nearby helps a young child settle and concentrate faster than a screen does, and it lets the tutor see the child's actual school materials directly. This is IB Gram's lead mode across Gurgaon for exactly this age group.

Online lessons work well once a routine is established, and suit families dealing with evening traffic on Sohna Road or through Cyber City, a rescheduled slot that only fits a narrow window, or a family away from Gurgaon for a short stretch. A shared screen handles reading practice, phonics and simple maths comfortably, though a young child's attention drops faster on screen than in person, so online PYP sessions tend to run shorter with more frequent changes of activity to hold focus.

Hybrid, mostly home tuition with online used when a specific week needs it, is how most regular arrangements in Gurgaon actually run after the first month or two. It keeps materials and rapport consistent while giving both sides a practical way to keep a session rather than cancel it outright. The trade-off is that hybrid needs one clear rule agreed in advance, home as default, online as the fallback, rather than a fresh negotiation every week.

Starting online-only is the one pattern that tends to underperform at this age: a child who has never met their tutor in person often takes longer to warm up on a screen. Two or three home sessions first, then shifting balance toward online if that suits the family better, generally settles faster than the reverse.

contentBlocks.heading: What Should You Ask the Tutor Before Committing to IB PYP Tuition?
contentBlocks.body:
Before the trial, ask how the tutor would plan a session around your child's current unit of inquiry, how they handle a child who is tired or unfocused, and how they will report back after each session; a specialist answers all three concretely, while a generalist tends to talk in general terms about building confidence without specifics. IB Gram has already checked the tutor's profile and PYP-relevant experience before shortlisting them, but these questions are still worth asking directly, since a written profile cannot show you how someone actually teaches a five-year-old.

During the trial itself, watch rather than just listen: does the tutor talk to your child directly, adjust when attention wanders, and use language a young learner can follow without talking down to them. A tutor who spends the session mostly addressing the parent, or who runs through a fixed script regardless of how the child responds, is showing you something important about how regular sessions will actually go.

After the trial, ask for a short, specific read: what the tutor noticed, where they would start, and roughly what frequency they would suggest and why. A vague "it went well" is not useful information; a tutor who can point to one or two concrete observations from a single session, and explain the reasoning behind a suggested starting point, is worth trusting with a regular arrangement.

If any of this feels off, IB Gram can offer a different tutor before any regular schedule is fixed. Nothing about a trial obliges a family to continue, and switching after one trial that did not click is far simpler than switching a few months into a regular arrangement.

contentBlocks.heading: Specialist or Generalist: How Do You Tell the Difference?
contentBlocks.body:
Choosing well matters because IB PYP tuition in Gurgaon is a long-term relationship, not a one-off session, and the clearest tell up front is language. A specialist PYP tutor talks naturally about units of inquiry, the learner profile and transdisciplinary themes because these are the vocabulary of their actual work; a generalist primary tutor, even a capable one, tends to talk about "topics" and "chapters" instead, borrowing the language of a textbook-led curriculum that the PYP does not use. Neither vocabulary makes someone a bad tutor, but only one of them means they have actually worked inside this programme.

The second tell is how they plan a lesson. Ask a specialist to sketch a session around a named unit, say How We Organize Ourselves, and they will describe building vocabulary, asking open-ended questions and connecting the topic to something the child already knows, rather than opening a workbook to a random page. A generalist, asked the same question, usually falls back to "I'll see what the child needs that day," which sounds flexible but often means no real plan tied to the unit at all.

IB Gram's shortlisting reflects this distinction directly: tutors are matched to a family based on stated PYP experience, not just general primary tutoring background, and the free trial class exists specifically so a family can verify that match for themselves rather than trust a written profile alone. A tutor with years of experience in CBSE or ICSE primary teaching is not automatically a PYP specialist, even though the age group overlaps; the programme's structure is genuinely different, and it shows within the first ten minutes of a trial session.

None of this means a generalist tutor is never the right call. A family whose child mainly needs raw reading or number practice, with little reference to the current unit, may do perfectly well with a strong generalist at a lower cost structure. The distinction matters most when a child is specifically struggling to connect with how the PYP teaches, in which case a specialist's familiarity with units of inquiry and the learner profile is the thing actually worth paying for.

contentBlocks.heading: How Do You Judge IB PYP Tuition Progress After Four Weeks?
contentBlocks.body:
After four weeks of regular IB PYP tuition, expect specific, describable change rather than a transformed child: perhaps more willingness to read aloud without prompting, steadier handwriting, a question about the current unit brought up unprompted at dinner, or simply less resistance to sitting down for the session. A tutor should be able to name two or three such moments when IB Gram checks in around the one-month mark, not just report that "things are going well."

If nothing has shifted at all after a full month of consistent sessions, that is worth raising directly rather than waiting it out. Sometimes the fix is small, a change of time slot, a different balance of activities, more movement built into the session for a restless child, and sometimes it means the tutor is not the right specialist match after all, in which case IB Gram can offer an alternative.

It helps to separate two different things a family sometimes conflates: enjoyment and progress. A child who loves their tutor but shows no measurable change in reading or number confidence is not necessarily making progress, and a child who grumbles about sessions but is visibly more capable a month in may be doing exactly what the tuition is meant to do. Ask the tutor about both, not just whether the child likes the sessions.

No tutor can guarantee a specific outcome or a particular grade equivalent, since the PYP does not grade in that sense at all. What steady tuition reliably offers is consistent attention to a child's actual gaps, tracked and adjusted every four to six weeks rather than left to run unexamined for a full term.

After the trial, agree a weekly frequency that matches what the child actually needs right now, not a fixed default, and expect IB Gram to check in around the one-month mark on how it is going. faqs.question: Is a live online group class a reasonable alternative to one-to-one tuition?

faqs.question: Should we stay with a tutor found through a personal recommendation instead?

faqs.question: What happens if there is no progress at all after a month?

faqs.question: Do sessions follow the school's term calendar?
faqs.answer: They should. Units of inquiry run for several weeks each, and a tuition plan that ignores this quickly falls out of step with what the child is actually doing in class. Term breaks, festival holidays and, in the final year, the run-up to the PYP exhibition all compress the weeks around them, so a fixed weekly slot that never flexes tends to clash with exactly these periods. faqs.question: Can tuition help specifically with the PYP exhibition?
faqs.answer: Yes, within limits. In the final year, tuition can shift to support research skills, organising ideas and rehearsing a presentation for the PYP exhibition, alongside any remaining subject gaps, since the exhibition draws on skills built across the whole programme. A tutor should coach the process, asking questions, helping structure ideas, rather than producing the research or the argument themselves; the exhibition is meant to be student-led, and tuition that crosses into doing the work undermines that.

IB Gram matches families with tutors experienced specifically with young learners, not simply any available tutor, because patience, pacing and reading a child's mood matter as much as subject knowledge at this age. contentBlocks.heading: Getting a Home Tutor Matched for Your PYP Child in Gurgaon
contentBlocks.body:
For PYP, most queries come from a parent who has just seen a unit of inquiry summary from school and is not sure how to support it at home, or from a parent whose child needs steadier one-to-one attention with early reading or numbers than a classroom of twenty can give. IB Gram's matching process for a home tutor is built to be quick, because a five-year-old does not wait patiently while paperwork happens.

1. Send a query or book a free consultation, telling us your child's age, current unit of inquiry or subject focus, school, and your sector or society.
2. IB Gram asks about your child's current stage: pre-reading, early reading, numeracy foundations, or supporting a specific unit of inquiry or the PYP exhibition if your child is in the final year.
3. We shortlist verified tutors experienced with young learners in this age range, not simply any available tutor.
4. A trial session is arranged at home, so you can watch how the tutor works with your child before committing to anything regular.
5. If the fit works, we set a consistent weekly slot; if it does not, ask us for a different tutor and we shortlist again.

For very young children, the tutor matters as much as the subject. A tutor who is warm and patient with a six-year-old but has never actually taught inside a PYP classroom will still miss what the unit of inquiry is asking for, so we match on both temperament and PYP familiarity, not one or the other. This is precisely why an IB PYP home tutor in Gurgaon found through a platform that checks both matters more than one found through a casual referral.

contentBlocks.heading: What the PYP Actually Looks Like at Home
contentBlocks.body:
The Primary Years Programme runs from age 3 to age 12 and does not look like a subject timetable the way CBSE or a senior IB programme does. Learning is organised around six transdisciplinary themes: Who We Are; Where We Are in Place and Time; How We Express Ourselves; How The World Works; How We Organize Ourselves; and Sharing The Planet. Each theme runs as a unit of inquiry lasting several weeks, pulling together literacy, numeracy and social studies under one central idea, rather than teaching them as separate subjects.

A home tutor working within this structure supports the unit the class is currently on rather than running a parallel curriculum, since a child exploring How The World Works through a science-based unit benefits more from a tutor reinforcing that vocabulary and thinking than from an unrelated worksheet. Alongside academic content, PYP schools track the ten attributes of the IB learner profile, inquirer, thinker, communicator, risk-taker, knowledgeable, principled, caring, open-minded, balanced and reflective, and a good home tutor notices and encourages these habits in how a session is run, not just in what is taught.

There are no external examinations at this stage, which surprises some parents moving from a board-exam mindset, and it means a home tutor's job is rarely exam preparation. In the final year of PYP, students complete the PYP exhibition, a collaborative, student-led inquiry project drawing on everything learned across the programme, and a tutor can support the research and presentation skills involved without taking over the work.

contentBlocks.heading: Units of Inquiry, Early Literacy and Numeracy at Home
contentBlocks.body:
Because PYP does not split into separate exam subjects the way later programmes do, home tuition mostly works across three areas: supporting the current unit of inquiry, building early literacy, and building early numeracy, with the balance shifting as a child grows through the programme.

For the youngest learners, roughly ages 3 to 6, home literacy support usually means phonics, sight-word recognition, and reading aloud together, while home numeracy support means number sense, counting, and simple pattern recognition, built through games and concrete materials rather than worksheets alone. A home tutor working with a child this young needs patience more than subject depth, and a 30 to 40 minute session, not a full hour, usually suits attention spans at this stage.

As children move through the middle and later PYP years, roughly ages 7 to 12, home sessions can support the specific unit of inquiry directly: helping a child research for How We Express Ourselves, structure a piece of writing for a unit on communication, or work through a maths concept the class has just covered. Session length can stretch towards 45 to 60 minutes as concentration improves, though even at age 11 or 12, PYP home tuition tends to stay shorter than an MYP or DP lesson.

In the final year, preparing for the PYP exhibition adds a research and presentation dimension: a tutor can help a child organise findings, practise explaining their thinking out loud, and build confidence presenting to an audience, all without doing the thinking for the child, since the exhibition is meant to be genuinely student-led.

contentBlocks.body:
Gurgaon has several international schools running the IB continuum from the early years, and PYP families juggle a calendar built around units of inquiry rather than a single annual exam. IB Gram is an independent platform and is not affiliated with any school named here, the International Baccalaureate, Cambridge International Education or Pearson Edexcel; we mention schools only to describe the calendar pressures families here manage.

A PYP school year typically moves through several units of inquiry, each lasting a few weeks, with a natural point of stocktaking, a class assembly, a learning showcase, or a portfolio review, at the end of each one. These showcases matter to young children in a way exam results do not to older students; a five-year-old who has nothing to show at a class assembly can feel it keenly, and a home tutor aware of the current unit and its showcase date can help a child prepare something they are proud of, not just academically ready.

Term breaks, festival holidays and school events also shape when home sessions make sense. A tutor who knows the school's actual term dates will plan around a half-day before a break rather than scheduling a full session a tired child cannot really use. Ask your child's homeroom teacher or the school's family handbook for the term calendar and the dates of unit showcases or exhibition milestones if your child is in the final year, and share that with your tutor early, since a session timed to a showcase in two weeks looks very different from a routine week.

contentBlocks.heading: Home, Online or Hybrid: What Works Best for a Young PYP Learner?
contentBlocks.body:
For PYP, home tuition is where IB Gram starts nearly every family, and for good reason: a young child concentrates better with a familiar adult at the same table, using real objects, books and materials, than staring at a screen for even 30 minutes. A home tutor can also read a young child's mood in a way a video call cannot, slowing down when a child is tired or restless rather than pushing through a fixed lesson plan.

Online lessons still have a place, particularly for slightly older PYP students, around ages 9 to 12, who are supporting a specific unit of inquiry with a specialist, or for families whose evening schedule or corridor makes a home visit hard on a given day. A shared screen works reasonably well for reading discussion or explaining a maths concept, though hands-on activities, building a model, running a simple experiment for a science-based unit, are genuinely better done in person.

Hybrid works for many families once the tutor and child know each other: home sessions form the regular rhythm, with the odd online session filling a gap when travel or timing does not work that week. For the youngest children, under about age 7, IB Gram generally recommends staying with home sessions consistently rather than mixing modes, since young children settle into routine more than they adapt to variety, and swapping formats week to week can undo some of the comfort a familiar home session builds.

contentBlocks.heading: How Is a PYP Home Tutor in Gurgaon Verified Before a Home Visit?
contentBlocks.body:
A PYP home tutor in Gurgaon on IB Gram is checked for experience with young learners specifically, not just a general teaching background, before they are shortlisted for your family, and you meet them for a trial session before any regular arrangement begins.

That check looks at whether a tutor has actually worked with children in this age range, since teaching a six-year-old is a different skill from teaching a Class 9 student; patience, pacing and the ability to hold attention through play matter as much as subject knowledge. We also confirm the tutor's familiarity with the PYP's inquiry-based approach, so they support a unit of inquiry rather than running an unrelated worksheet programme alongside it.

Before the first home visit, there is work worth doing yourself too. Ask about the tutor's experience with your child's specific age group, and ask what a typical first session with a young child looks like. Confirm your society's visitor registration and gate entry process with the tutor in advance, since arriving at a gate without prior registration can cost ten or fifteen minutes a young child spends waiting rather than learning. It is also reasonable, and common, for a parent to stay nearby or in the next room for the first few sessions with a very young child, until both child and tutor are comfortable.

Availability is subject to tutor schedule and level, and if the first trial does not feel right for your child, ask IB Gram for a different match.

contentBlocks.heading: What Does the First IB PYP Home Tutor Session Look Like?
contentBlocks.body:
The first session with an IB PYP home tutor is mostly about the tutor getting to know your child, not diving into a lesson plan. Expect the tutor to spend part of the first 20 to 30 minutes talking with your child, looking through a school book or portfolio if you have one, and gently gauging where they are with reading, numbers and their current unit of inquiry, before easing into any actual teaching.

A parent or another familiar adult should be reachable, and for a child under about age 7, present in the home for the whole session, even if not sitting at the table throughout. The study space matters more for young children than older ones: a consistent spot, a table at the right height, good light, and minimal distractions, works better than a bedroom with toys nearby or a shared family space with a television on.

Materials for the first session are simple: the child's current schoolbook or reading material if available, a notebook, basic stationery, and if your child has one, their portfolio or any recent unit of inquiry work. A tutor does not need much more than this to begin, and bringing too much material to a first session with a young child can be overwhelming rather than helpful.

Before the first visit, run through a short checklist. 1. Confirm the exact time and share gate or visitor details with the tutor in advance. 2. Set up a consistent, quiet space with a table and good light. 3. Keep the child's current schoolbook, reading material and any portfolio nearby. 4. Let your child know a new tutor is coming and what to expect, so the session does not feel sudden. 5. Plan to be home or nearby for the full first session, especially for a younger child.
items: The first session focuses on getting to know the child, not a full lesson plan.
A parent should be present in the home for the whole session under about age 7.
A consistent, well-lit study space works better than a bedroom or shared living area.

contentBlocks.heading: Is the Home Tutor Arrangement Actually Working for Your Child?
contentBlocks.body:
With a young PYP learner, progress looks different from a grade moving. In the first few weeks, look for a child who is more willing to read aloud, who mentions the tutor or the day's activity unprompted after school, or who approaches a maths game or a reading task with less resistance than before. These small behavioural signs often show up before any measurable academic change does, and they matter, because a child who dreads a session will not learn much from it regardless of how skilled the tutor is.

By around a month, ask the tutor directly what they have noticed: has reading fluency improved, is number sense stronger, is the child engaging more confidently with their current unit of inquiry. A tutor working well with a young child should be able to describe specific, small changes, not just say the sessions are going fine.

Be honest about what a home tutor cannot do. No tutor can guarantee a reading level or a particular outcome, and any promise of a fixed timeline for a young child should be treated carefully, since children this age progress unevenly, in bursts rather than a straight line. A tutor is also not a substitute for a paediatric or educational assessment if you are concerned about a genuine learning difficulty; in that case, raise it with the school first and treat tutoring as support alongside that, not instead of it.

If, after six to eight weeks, your child still resists sessions or you cannot name any specific change, ask IB Gram for a different tutor rather than assuming it will improve on its own. A good IB PYP home tutor in Gurgaon should welcome this kind of honest check-in rather than treat it as a challenge.

faqs.question: Is a home tutor really better than sending my child to a class outside?
faqs.answer: It depends on your child, but for most PYP-age children, a home tutor's individual attention and familiar setting tends to suit them better than an unfamiliar class outside, where a young child is one of several and the pace is not set around them specifically. A class outside can still work well for a sociable child who enjoys group activity, or when a family simply cannot arrange consistent home slots. Neither option is universally right; the honest answer is that a home tutor suits a child needing individual pace and comfort, and a class outside suits a child who does well in a group.

faqs.question: How is a PYP home tutor different from a school teacher's extra help?
faqs.answer: A school teacher's extra help, where it exists, is usually a short, general catch-up session inside the school day, aimed at the whole class or a small group, while a PYP home tutor works one-to-one, at your child's pace, on exactly the unit of inquiry or skill your child needs that week. A home tutor also has more time to notice and work on habits, like reading stamina or number confidence, that a busy classroom rarely has room for individually. The two are not competing; a home tutor typically reinforces what the school teacher has already introduced, rather than replacing it.

faqs.question: What if my child does not warm up to the tutor?
faqs.answer: Give it a fair few sessions before deciding, since many young children take a session or two to warm up to any new adult, home tutor or otherwise. If your child is still visibly uncomfortable after three or four sessions, tell IB Gram directly rather than persisting, and we will shortlist a different tutor whose temperament may suit your child better. Personality fit matters as much as teaching skill at this age, and there is no obligation to continue with a tutor your child is not warming up to.

contentBlocks.heading: How Does a Private IB PYP Arrangement Start in Gurgaon?
contentBlocks.body:
An IB PYP private tutor in Gurgaon works outside the school entirely, so the process starts with a conversation, not a classroom introduction. You tell IB Gram which school your child attends, their age and current unit of inquiry, and whether the family wants home tutoring, online lessons or a hybrid mix; IB Gram then shortlists a verified private tutor whose experience matches the Primary Years Programme rather than a general primary curriculum, and arranges a free trial class before anything is fixed.

Because the tutor is independent, nothing about the arrangement passes through the school. IB Gram does not ask which teacher your child has and does not coordinate with school staff on your behalf; that separation is part of what makes the arrangement private. Once a family confirms the trial went well, the tutor and parent agree a regular slot directly, usually one or two sessions a week to begin with, adjusted after the first month once the tutor has seen how the child works.

Most families ask for weekday evening slots once school activities finish, though a young PYP child tires earlier in the evening than an older sibling doing board-exam subjects, so a slot right after the school bus gets in often works better than a late one. A tutor covering Palam Vihar or the Golf Course Road corridor plans around Gurgaon's evening traffic when confirming a start time, and says plainly if a requested slot is not realistic rather than promising something that will get missed.

A private arrangement suits families who already know what they want fixed: no school liaison, no batch of other children, just consistent one-to-one home tutoring or online lessons for their own child. It suits less well a family still deciding whether their child needs help at all, since a paid trial with an independent tutor is a bigger first step than asking a school teacher a quick question at pickup.

contentBlocks.heading: What Does the IB Primary Years Programme Actually Involve?
contentBlocks.body:
The IB Primary Years Programme (PYP) runs from ages 3 to 12 and organises learning around six transdisciplinary themes: Who we are; Where we are in place and time; How we express ourselves; How the world works; How we organize ourselves; and Sharing the planet. Each theme runs as a unit of inquiry lasting several weeks, blending subjects instead of teaching them separately, and every unit is meant to develop one or more of the ten attributes of the IB learner profile alongside the subject content itself.

There are no external examinations at any point in the programme, which changes what a private tutor is actually there to support. A PYP tutor for a Gurgaon family is not preparing a child for a paper with a mark scheme; the tutor reinforces the thinking skills, reading stamina and number sense a unit of inquiry assumes the child already has, and closes gaps the classroom moves past quickly. In the final year, students complete the PYP exhibition, a collaborative, student-led inquiry project that draws on everything the programme has built up.

An independent private tutor works from the same theme and central idea the class is studying, without ever touching the school's own assessed tasks. If the current unit is How the World Works and the class is investigating simple machines, the tutor might build the child's vocabulary and observation skills around that theme at home, rather than write the child's inquiry journal entries or correct a piece of work the teacher will grade. That distinction, doing the groundwork instead of the graded task itself, is what keeps a private arrangement honest and useful rather than a shortcut.

Because PYP assessment is largely teacher-observed rather than tested, a private tutor's read on a child's progress depends on watching carefully across weeks, not on a single score. That makes the trial class and the first few regular sessions more important than they would be for an older child preparing for a graded paper: this is where a family sees whether the tutor actually understands how a unit of inquiry works, or is running a generic primary tutoring session with a PYP label on it.

Three more themes: How the world works; How we organize ourselves; Sharing the planet.
Ten attributes of the IB learner profile run through every unit of inquiry.
No external examinations anywhere in the Primary Years Programme.
The PYP exhibition is a student-led inquiry project completed in the final year.

contentBlocks.heading: Units of Inquiry, Early Literacy and the PYP Exhibition
contentBlocks.body:
Literacy and numeracy sit inside the units of inquiry rather than as separate timetabled subjects the way older students experience them. A private tutor supporting early literacy reads with the child, builds phonics or sight-word fluency depending on age, and talks through a picture book or an inquiry text the class is using, rather than working from an unrelated workbook. For numeracy, the tutor practises number sense, patterns and simple problem-solving in the same open-ended style the PYP classroom uses, so the child does not experience two contradictory styles of maths in the same week.

Attention spans at this age shape everything about how a session is structured. A five-year-old cannot sustain forty minutes of focused reading practice the way a ten-year-old preparing for the PYP exhibition can, so a private tutor working with a younger child breaks a session into several short activities with a change of task between them, while a session with an older PYP student can run longer and closer to independent work with the tutor coaching from the side.

Students in the final year of the programme complete the PYP exhibition, a collaborative, student-led inquiry into a real issue that the child helps choose and researches largely independently, presenting the findings to the school community. A private tutor's role here is narrow and should stay that way: helping the child research, organise ideas, rehearse the presentation and manage the workload across weeks, never producing content the child is meant to have found or argued themselves. Confusing support with authorship undermines the entire point of the exhibition.

Because a private tutor works with one child rather than a class, mapping to the school's own scheme of work matters more here than in a batch setting: a tutor who assumes every PYP classroom teaches units in the same order, or covers a central idea the same way, ends up teaching against what the child is learning at school that week rather than alongside it. Confirming the current unit and central idea with the parent before each block of sessions avoids that mismatch, and is one of the clearest signs of an IB PYP private tutor who actually knows the programme.

Numeracy practice mirrors the PYP's open-ended, inquiry-based style rather than drill sheets.

PYP exhibition support stays limited to research, organisation and rehearsal, never authorship.

contentBlocks.heading: School Calendars in Gurgaon and the Case for an Outside Tutor
contentBlocks.body:
IB Gram is an independent platform and is not affiliated with any school named here, the International Baccalaureate, Cambridge International Education or Pearson Edexcel. Families in Gurgaon whose children attend schools such as Pathways World School Aravali, Pathways School Gurgaon, Lancers International School, Scottish High International School, GD Goenka World School, Heritage Xperiential Learning School, The Shri Ram School Aravali or DPS International Edge follow a school year built around term breaks, unit changes and, in the final PYP year, exhibition milestones; the school names appear here only as local context, never as a claim about which programme any of them runs.

A private tutor arranging home tuition works around that calendar rather than setting one of their own. A unit of inquiry typically runs several weeks before the class moves to the next theme, and a tutor who does not track that shift ends up reinforcing content the child has already left behind. Parents are usually the fastest way for a tutor to know a unit has changed, since a private tutor has no direct line to the school and should not be expected to build one.

Festival breaks, sports days, parent-teacher meetings and the run-up to the PYP exhibition all compress the weeks around them, and a private tutor who insists on an unchanged weekly slot through a school's busiest fortnight is not reading the calendar correctly. The more useful approach is to treat the schedule as a default that flexes around three or four predictable pressure points a term, agreed in advance rather than negotiated week by week.

This is also where the case for an outside tutor over the child's own teacher becomes concrete: a teacher already stretched across parent meetings, report writing and exhibition supervision for an entire class has little capacity left to also plan and deliver a private session for one family, however good the intention. An independent private tutor's only calendar commitment is your child.

contentBlocks.heading: Home Tutoring, Online or Hybrid: Which Suits a Private PYP Arrangement?
contentBlocks.body:
Home tutoring is the default for an IB PYP private tutor in Gurgaon, because young children concentrate better in a familiar room with their own materials close by than in front of a screen, and a parent can quietly observe without disrupting the session. A tutor working at home also sees the child's actual homework folder, reading books and unit-of-inquiry materials directly, which speeds up how quickly the sessions align with what the school is doing that week.

Online lessons are the honest alternative when travel makes a home visit impractical: a Manesar family on a weekday evening, a rescheduled session that only fits into a narrow window, or a family travelling out of Gurgaon for a fortnight. A shared screen works well for reading together, phonics and simple maths problems, but a young child's attention on a screen drops faster than it does in person, so online PYP sessions run shorter and lean more on the tutor keeping things interactive minute to minute.

Hybrid, home sessions most weeks with online filling in when needed, is what most private PYP arrangements in Gurgaon actually settle into after the first month. It keeps the relationship and materials consistent while giving both sides a way out of a single clashing evening without cancelling the week's session altogether. The trade-off is coordination: a hybrid schedule needs a clear default, home tuition, and a clear fallback, online, agreed once rather than negotiated fresh every week.

What does not work well for this age group is treating online as the primary mode from the start. A young PYP learner who has never met their tutor in person often takes longer to settle into an online-first relationship, so families who expect to lean on video calls are usually better served starting with two or three home sessions before shifting the balance online.

Online lessons: best for travel-heavy weeks, shorter sessions, more screen-interactive teaching.

contentBlocks.heading: How Are Private Tutors Verified Before They Meet Your Child?
contentBlocks.body:
IB Gram verifies an IB PYP private tutor's profile, subject and programme background before shortlisting them to a family, and only shortlists tutors whose experience genuinely matches the Primary Years Programme rather than general primary tutoring. That shortlist is the starting point, not the end of the parent's own checking: a family meeting a new adult who will spend time alone with their child should still ask direct questions and watch the trial class carefully.

Before the first home session, ask the tutor to talk through how they would approach the child's current unit of inquiry; a tutor who cannot describe transdisciplinary teaching in plain terms, or who talks only about worksheets and tests, is probably not a PYP specialist however confident they sound. Ask, too, how they handle a session where the child is tired, upset or simply uninterested that day, since with a five- or six-year-old this happens more often than with an older student.

During the trial class, a parent should stay within earshot, if not in the room, particularly for a first meeting. Notice whether the tutor talks to the child directly rather than only to the parent, whether they adjust when the child loses focus, and whether they leave with a clear, honest read on what the child needs next rather than a vague compliment. If any of this feels off, IB Gram can offer a different tutor; nothing obliges a family to continue past a trial that did not work.

Confidentiality works both ways in a private arrangement. The tutor should not discuss the child's learning gaps with anyone outside the family, and in turn a family should tell the tutor directly, not through a third party, if something in the arrangement needs to change. Put this expectation in writing alongside the schedule and cancellation terms, so it is not left to assumption on either side.

contentBlocks.heading: Your Child's Own Teacher, or an Independent Private Tutor?
contentBlocks.body:
Some Gurgaon families are offered private lessons by their child's own class or subject teacher, usually with good intentions and a genuine wish to help. It is worth thinking through before agreeing: the same person who is teaching, observing and reporting on your child during the school day would also be paid privately by you outside it, which is a conflict of interest even when nobody involved intends anything improper. An IB PYP private tutor found through IB Gram has no role in how your child is assessed at school, which removes that conflict entirely.

This is not a claim that a teacher tutoring privately is dishonest. It is a structural point: a teacher forming judgements about a child's learner-profile attributes, effort and progress has an interest, even an unconscious one, in how well the private sessions they are also paid for appear to be working. An independent tutor's only relationship with the school is indirect, through the family, so the same tension does not arise.

An independent private tutor also needs to work from the school's actual scheme of work rather than a generic curriculum, and this is where the mapping matters practically, not just as a principle. Ask the tutor to confirm, before each block of sessions, the current transdisciplinary theme, the central idea if the school shares one, and roughly what the class is producing that unit. The tutor builds sessions around that without ever touching graded or assessed schoolwork directly; supporting the thinking behind a task is different from doing the task.

Put the practical terms in writing early: the weekly schedule and what counts as enough cancellation notice, how progress will be communicated (a short note after each session works well for this age), what stays confidential and to whom, and what happens if either side wants to end the arrangement. None of this needs to be formal or lengthy, but a private arrangement without any of it written down tends to drift into misunderstanding by the second month, usually over cancellations or unclear expectations rather than anything more serious.

contentBlocks.heading: How Much Progress Should a Family Expect, and What Are Its Limits?
contentBlocks.body:
Because the PYP has no tests to mark, progress with a private tutor shows up as behaviour rather than a score: a child who used to avoid reading aloud starting to volunteer, one who rushed through maths now checking their own working, questions at home about the current unit of inquiry that were not there before. A tutor should be able to describe specific moments like this after three or four sessions, not just say the child is doing well.

No IB PYP private tutor in Gurgaon can guarantee a particular outcome, and one who promises one should be treated with more caution, not less. What a good private arrangement reliably delivers is consistent, focused attention on one child's actual gaps, which is harder to get inside a classroom of twenty or a batch of ten. That is a real and useful thing on its own; it is not the same as a guarantee.

Limits are worth naming honestly too. A private tutor is not a substitute for the school's own teacher, cannot change how the school assesses the PYP exhibition, and should never be asked to write or correct a piece of graded schoolwork on the child's behalf. If a child's struggle looks like it needs an educational assessment rather than tutoring, for attention, reading or another learning difference, a private tutor should say so and suggest the family raise it with the school rather than quietly working around it.

Review progress properly every four to six weeks rather than judging week to week, since a five-year-old's concentration varies day to day for reasons that have nothing to do with the tutor. Ask for two or three concrete examples of what has changed, and be direct if nothing has: switching tutors or pausing the arrangement is a reasonable response to a genuine lack of movement, not a failure on the family's part.

contentBlocks.heading: Starting a Private IB PYP Tutor Arrangement in Gurgaon
contentBlocks.body:
Getting started takes one message: tell IB Gram the child's school, age, current unit of inquiry if you know it, and whether you want home tutoring, online lessons or a hybrid mix. IB Gram asks a few follow-up questions about schedule and location, then shortlists a verified IB PYP private tutor whose background fits the Primary Years Programme specifically.

The first session is the free trial class, arranged at home, online or hybrid depending on preference and subject to tutor availability. Come with the child's reading book, any notes on the current unit and a rough sense of the areas you would like the tutor to focus on, though a general starting point is fine too if you are not sure yet.

After the trial, agree the regular arrangement directly with the tutor: weekly schedule, cancellation notice, how progress updates will be shared and what stays confidential. Put it in writing, even briefly, so nothing is left to memory two months in. If the fit is not right after the trial, or after a few regular sessions, ask IB Gram for a different match; that is a normal part of finding the right person, not an inconvenience.

From there, sessions settle into a rhythm around the school's own calendar, reviewed every four to six weeks and adjusted as the child's units of inquiry change. Nothing about a private arrangement needs to feel complicated once the first few basics are agreed.

faqs.question: Will a private tutor follow what my child is actually doing at school?

Private arrangements without anything written down tend to drift into misunderstanding by the second month, almost always over cancellations or unclear expectations rather than anything more serious. Put it in writing early, even briefly, so nothing depends on memory once the routine settles in.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram do anything different from just finding us a private tutor?
faqs.answer: Yes. IB Gram verifies a tutor's profile and Primary Years Programme experience before shortlisting them, arranges a free trial class so you see the tutor work with your child before committing, and stays reachable if the fit is not right so you can ask for a different match. faqs.question: How much does an IB PYP private tutor cost?

faqs.question: Can the tutor travel to our home in DLF Phase 5 on weekday evenings?

Confirm the tower and flat number with the tutor in advance so the security desk has it ready. faqs.question: What if the tutor and my child are not a fit after the trial?
faqs.answer: Say so, and ask IB Gram for a different tutor; this is a normal, expected part of finding the right match, not an awkward exception. A trial class exists specifically so you are not committing to a regular schedule before you have seen how the tutor works with your child. The same applies later, a few weeks or months in: if progress has genuinely stalled or the relationship is not working, switching is a reasonable decision, not a failure on your part or the tutor's.

faqs.question: Should I stay in the room during home sessions?
faqs.answer: For a first session with a young child, staying within earshot, if not in the room, is sensible and most tutors expect it. Watch whether the tutor talks to your child directly rather than only to you, and whether they adjust when the child loses focus, which happens more with five- and six-year-olds than with older students. Beyond the first couple of sessions, most families step back once trust is established, though this is a personal decision and there is no fixed rule either way for a private arrangement.

faqs.question: What happens if we need to cancel a home session at short notice?
faqs.answer: Agree the cancellation notice period upfront, in writing, alongside the weekly schedule, so this is not negotiated fresh every time it comes up. Most private arrangements settle on a day or so of notice as reasonable for either side, though school events, illness or a sudden change of plan are common enough with young children that some flexibility helps both the family and the tutor. Families in Manesar and along NH-48 south, where a home visit already depends on traffic, often find it easiest to shift a short-notice cancellation to an online session rather than losing the week's lesson entirely.

faqs.question: My child has no tests in the PYP; how do we know a private tutor is actually helping?
faqs.answer: Watch for specific behaviour changes rather than a score: more willingness to read aloud, checking their own maths working, unprompted questions about the current unit of inquiry at home. A tutor who cannot point to concrete examples like these after three or four sessions is not tracking progress properly, whatever they say about the child doing well. No tutor can guarantee a particular outcome, but consistent, focused attention on your child's actual gaps is a real benefit worth reviewing every four to six weeks, honestly, rather than assuming it is working.

faqs.question: Is a private tutor better than sending my child to a coaching centre batch?
faqs.answer: It depends what you need. A private tutor gives full, one-to-one attention and confidentiality outside the school, which suits a child who needs focused, individual work on specific gaps; a coaching centre batch usually costs less per session and can work for a child who benefits from being alongside peers, though it rarely maps closely to any one school's actual unit of inquiry. Neither is universally better: it is worth being honest about which trade-off, attention versus cost, matters more for your particular child before choosing.

faqs.question: Can a private tutor help with the PYP exhibition in the final year?
faqs.answer: Within limits, yes. A private tutor can help the child research, organise ideas and rehearse a presentation for the PYP exhibition, but should never produce content, an argument or a piece of writing the child is meant to have found or developed themselves, since that undermines the entire point of the exhibition as a student-led inquiry. If a tutor's exhibition help starts to look like doing the project rather than supporting the child through it, that is worth raising directly with them.

A private tutor gives full, one-to-one attention and confidentiality outside the school, which suits a child who needs focused, individual work on specific gaps; a coaching centre batch usually costs less per session and can work for a child who benefits from being alongside peers, though it rarely maps closely to any one school's actual unit of inquiry. Neither is universally better: it is worth being honest about which trade-off, attention versus cost, matters more for your particular child before choosing.

mainEntity.name: Can a private tutor help with the PYP exhibition in the final year?

acceptedAnswer.text: Within limits, yes. A private tutor can help the child research, organise ideas and rehearse a presentation for the PYP exhibition, but should never produce content, an argument or a piece of writing the child is meant to have found or developed themselves, since that undermines the entire point of the exhibition as a student-led inquiry. If a tutor's exhibition help starts to look like doing the project rather than supporting the child through it, that is worth raising directly with them.

contentBlocks.heading: The PYP Curriculum an Online Tutor Actually Works With
contentBlocks.body:
The Primary Years Programme covers ages 3 to 12 and organises learning around six transdisciplinary themes rather than separate subjects: Who We Are; Where We Are In Place And Time; How We Express Ourselves; How The World Works; How We Organize Ourselves; and Sharing The Planet. An online tutor needs to know which unit of inquiry your child's class is currently working through, since a session disconnected from that unit feels like a different subject entirely to a young child trying to hold two unrelated threads in their head at once.

Screen-based teaching works better for some parts of this curriculum than others. Discussing a unit's central idea, talking through vocabulary, reviewing a piece of writing, or working through a maths concept using an on-screen whiteboard all translate reasonably well to video. The ten attributes of the IB learner profile, inquirer, thinker, communicator, risk-taker, knowledgeable, principled, caring, open-minded, balanced and reflective, still shape how a good online tutor runs a session, encouraging a child to ask questions and reflect out loud rather than just answer prompts.

There are no external examinations in the PYP, so an online tutor's role is almost never exam preparation; it is steady support for the unit of inquiry and for literacy and numeracy foundations. In the final year, students complete the PYP exhibition, a collaborative, student-led inquiry project, and an online tutor can support research and rehearsal of a presentation over video, though the collaborative planning with classmates and the final presentation itself happen at school, not on a screen with the tutor.

contentBlocks.heading: What Suits a Screen: Literacy, Numeracy and Units of Inquiry
contentBlocks.body:
Some tasks suit a screen well. Reading a passage together and discussing it, explaining a maths method step by step on a shared digital whiteboard, reviewing a piece of writing line by line with visible annotations, and talking through vocabulary for a unit of inquiry all work close to as well online as in person, because they rely on verbal explanation and visible working rather than physical manipulation.

Other tasks do not translate well. Early phonics work with a child under about 6, where a tutor needs to watch mouth shapes and physically guide a pencil grip, is genuinely harder over video. Hands-on unit of inquiry activities, building a simple model, running a basic experiment for a How The World Works unit, sorting physical objects for an early maths concept, lose most of their value on a screen, since the whole point is manipulation, not observation. A tutor aware of this will suggest sending simple physical materials in advance so the child still handles something real during the session, rather than pretending a screen-based substitute is equivalent.

For early numeracy specifically, online sessions work best with printed or physical counters the family has ready beforehand, since pointing at a screen is a weak substitute for moving an actual object. For early literacy, a physical book in the child's hands, held up to the camera or read alongside a shared digital text, keeps the session closer to how reading is actually taught in class.

The honest rule is this: anything primarily verbal, explanation, discussion, reviewing written work, works online. Anything primarily physical, fine motor practice, hands-on unit activities, needs either physical materials prepared in advance or is better done in person.

contentBlocks.heading: Online, Home or Hybrid: Which Suits a Young PYP Learner?
contentBlocks.body:
Online lessons work well for PYP when the family's situation calls for it: a specific specialist who is not based nearby, an evening schedule that a home visit cannot reliably fit, or simply wanting to remove travel time from an already short session for a young child. A shared digital whiteboard, an on-screen document, and a webcam angled to see both the child and their working page let a tutor teach most of the PYP curriculum effectively, provided the connection holds up.

Home tuition remains a genuine alternative worth considering, especially for the youngest PYP children, roughly under age 7, who often concentrate better with a tutor physically present, and for any session built around hands-on unit of inquiry activities, model-building, simple experiments, or sorting physical objects, that a screen cannot properly replace. If your child is easily distracted on video calls, or if early phonics work needs close, physical guidance, home tuition may suit better than persisting with online out of habit.

Hybrid, mixing online for most weeks with an occasional home session timed around a hands-on unit or a showcase, is a genuinely useful middle path many Gurgaon families settle into once they understand their child's actual needs. The honest comparison is this: online wins on flexibility, access to specialists and removing travel time; home wins on holding a young child's attention and handling physical, hands-on work; hybrid takes the best of both once you know which weeks need which.

contentBlocks.heading: What Actually Makes an Online PYP Lesson Work?
contentBlocks.body:
A good online PYP lesson depends more on preparation than on the tutor's skill alone, particularly for a young child whose attention is the scarcest resource in the room. Before the first session, run through a practical setup checklist: a laptop or tablet, not a phone, propped at a stable height so the camera shows both your child's face and their working page; a stable internet connection tested at the actual lesson time, not just once earlier in the day; headphones if the household is noisy, since background sound is more distracting for a young child than for an older student; good, even lighting so the tutor can actually see the child's face and expressions, not just a silhouette; and a quiet, consistent spot, ideally the same one each session, free of a television or siblings playing nearby.

Beyond equipment, a few habits make a real difference. Keep session length realistic: 30 minutes for the youngest children, stretching towards 45 minutes as concentration improves with age, since a tired child on a screen disengages faster than a tired child at a physical table. Have materials ready before the session starts, a notebook, basic stationery, the current schoolbook, so the first five minutes are not spent searching for a pencil while the tutor waits.

A shared digital whiteboard or annotation tool matters more for PYP than people expect, since a young child benefits from seeing ideas written and drawn in real time, not just hearing them explained. Ask your tutor which tool they use and do a brief test run before the first proper lesson, so the actual session starts smoothly rather than troubleshooting software in front of a five-year-old losing patience.

contentBlocks.heading: How Do You Know Online Tutoring Is Working Within Three Sessions?
contentBlocks.body:
Within three sessions, you should be able to tell whether online is genuinely working for your child, and it is worth checking deliberately rather than assuming it either way. Watch whether your child stays reasonably engaged for the agreed session length, whether they can follow the tutor's explanation without constant repetition, and whether they seem tired or restless earlier than expected, since screen fatigue shows up faster in young children than in-person fatigue does.

Ask your child directly, in simple terms, what they did with the tutor and whether they enjoyed it; a vague answer after three sessions is itself useful information. Ask the tutor too: have they noticed the connection holding steady, is your child responding well to the shared whiteboard, and is there a particular type of activity, reading aloud, a maths game, discussing the unit of inquiry, that is working better than others so far.

Be honest about limits. Online tutoring is not the right fit for every child; some young children simply do not engage well over video regardless of the tutor's skill, and persisting for months hoping it will click can waste time better spent on a home tutor instead. No tutor can guarantee a particular outcome or pace of progress, online or otherwise, and a young child's development happens unevenly, so judge the arrangement on engagement and small, specific signs, not on comparing weeks directly against each other. A good IB PYP online tutor in Gurgaon should treat an honest check-in like this as normal, not a challenge.

If, after three to four sessions, your child is consistently disengaged or resistant, that is a fair point to ask IB Gram about switching to a home or hybrid arrangement rather than continuing online out of momentum.

faqs.question: Does online tutoring really work for a young PYP child, or is it just a compromise?
faqs.answer: It genuinely works for most PYP-age children, provided the setup is right and the tutor has real experience teaching young learners over video, but it is not automatically a substitute for in-person attention for every child. Discussion, reading, writing review and maths explanation on a shared whiteboard translate well to a screen. Early phonics work and hands-on unit of inquiry activities translate less well and may need materials prepared in advance or an occasional home session instead. Judge it on your own child's engagement over the first few sessions rather than assuming either way in advance.

faqs.question: What if our internet connection is unreliable during a session?
faqs.answer: Test your connection at the actual time of day the lesson runs, since evening bandwidth in a crowded society can differ from a quiet afternoon, and flag persistent issues to IB Gram so we can look at alternatives. An occasional dropped call is normal and most tutors simply reconnect and continue; a session repeatedly disrupted is worth raising directly, since it may point to a router placement issue, a need for a wired connection, or, if it continues, a reason to consider a hybrid arrangement with occasional home sessions instead.

faqs.question: How is an online lesson different from a video call with a relative?
faqs.answer: An online PYP lesson is structured and purposeful in a way a casual video call is not: the tutor follows what the school's current unit of inquiry actually needs, uses a shared digital whiteboard to show working and diagrams, and keeps the session paced to your child's attention span rather than open-ended chatting. The tutor also comes prepared with materials and a plan for the session, checks in on specific skills like reading fluency or number sense, and gives you feedback afterwards, none of which a casual family video call is built to do.

faqs.question: Can the tutor still support hands-on unit of inquiry work online?
faqs.answer: Yes, within limits: a tutor can talk your child through a hands-on unit activity, demonstrate a step on camera, and guide your child through the same activity at home if you have gathered simple materials in advance. What an online tutor cannot do is physically guide a child's hands or observe fine detail the way an in-person tutor can, so for unit weeks built heavily around hands-on activities, some families schedule an occasional home session instead, or send photos of the completed work afterwards for feedback.

faqs.question: What if my child gets distracted or restless on screen?
faqs.answer: Keep early online sessions short, around 30 minutes, and build up gradually rather than starting at 45 minutes and hoping attention holds. A tutor experienced with young children will build in short breaks, vary activities between talking, writing and the shared whiteboard, and notice restlessness before it becomes disengagement. If distraction persists across several sessions despite this, it is worth reviewing the time of day, tiredness after school, or background noise at home, and raising it with IB Gram, since a different tutor's pacing style or a switch to home sessions may suit your child better.

faqs.question: Does someone need to be home during an online lesson?
faqs.answer: For a child under about age 7, yes, a parent or familiar adult should generally be nearby during an online lesson, even if not visible on camera, in case the child needs quick reassurance or help with the shared screen. Older PYP children, roughly ages 9 to 12, often manage an online session independently once they are used to the format and the tutor. Sitting in the next room rather than directly in view usually works well, since a hovering parent can sometimes make a young child more self-conscious on camera.

faqs.question: How soon can an online tutor start?
faqs.answer: Start times depend on tutor availability for your child's age group and preferred schedule, so send your query as early as you can rather than the week you need help. Once IB Gram has your requirements, shortlisting a suitable online tutor and arranging a first trial session usually happens quickly, subject to the matched tutor's own schedule. If you have a specific date in mind, an upcoming showcase or the start of a new unit of inquiry, mention it in your first message so we can prioritise accordingly.

faqs.question: What happens if an online session is missed?
faqs.answer: Tell your tutor and IB Gram as early as you can, and the session is rescheduled to another day that week where the tutor's schedule allows, subject to availability. Missed online sessions happen for the same reasons any session does, illness, an unexpected evening commitment, a technical problem that could not be resolved in time, and an occasional reschedule is normal. What matters more is not letting missed sessions pile up without a plan, since young children lose momentum with unit of inquiry work faster than older students do.

faqs.question: Is a recorded video course a good substitute for live online tutoring?
faqs.answer: A recorded video course can be a reasonable low-cost supplement, but it is not a substitute for live tutoring for a PYP-age child, since it cannot respond to your child's specific unit of inquiry, answer a question in the moment, or notice when a concept has not landed. It suits a family wanting extra, always-available practice material alongside tutoring, not instead of it. Live online one-to-one, by contrast, adapts to exactly what your child needs that week, which matters more at this age than at almost any later stage of school.
